ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was approved by the joint Institutional Review Board of Taipei Medical University (N201910050).
As for Experiment 1, the same IRB approval applied and the same apparatus were used.
Methods: Across two experiments, participants completed a two-alternative forced-choice discrimination task embedded within a Posner cueing paradigm, utilizing adaptive staircases.
Four participants were excluded according to the criteria described below, leaving a final sample size of 15.
All participants had normal or correctedto-normal vision, provided written informed consent, and received monetary compensation.
Participants were asked to report if they had consciously seen the figure.
Participants were instructed to guess the target identity whenever they reported not seeing it.
Participants were asked to identify the shape of the target stimulus and report if they had seen it.
Participants were informed that the spatial cue (dot) predicted the target location on most trials.

Overall, four participants and ten blocks of trials (across 8 participants) were excluded from analysis, resulting in a final sample of 15 participants and 65 blocks of trials in total (a necessary loss of 31% of unstable datasets).
All of these participants had already agreed to participate in Experiment 1 and thus were familiar with the task.
All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, gave written informed consent, and received monetary compensation.
Participants completed the same visual discrimination task described in Experiment 1.
Participants were asked to identify the shape of the target stimulus and report if they had seen it.
Participants were informed that the spatial cue (dot) predicted the target location on most trials.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: While endogenous attention is known to influence visual metacognition, it remains unclear whether these effects occur without altering perceptual performance, and what specific role the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) plays in mediating them.

Objective: We investigated whether spatial attention modulates subjective visibility and metacognitive efficiency independently of perceptual sensitivity (d′), and whether the DLPFC contributes to these effects.
Methods: Across two experiments, participants completed a two-alternative forced-choice discrimination task embedded within a Posner cueing paradigm, utilizing adaptive staircases.
We assessed reaction times, signal detection metrics, subjective visibility ratings, and metacognitive efficiency.
In Experiment 2, this task was performed following continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS) targeting either the bilateral DLPFC or an active control site (primary somatosensory cortex, S1).

In Experiment 1, invalid cues prolonged reaction times, shifted response bias, and impaired metacognitive efficiency, without affecting overall accuracy, subjective visibility, or perceptual sensitivity.

In Experiment 2, whereas these attentional effects persisted following control S1-cTBS, they were significantly disrupted following DLPFC-cTBS, despite objective perceptual performance remaining stable.
Furthermore, trial-bytrial analyses indicated that DLPFC disruption impairs adaptive metacognitive updating.
Conclusions: Endogenous spatial attention modulates visual metacognitive efficiency independently of objective perceptual sensitivity.

Notably, our neuromodulatory findings suggest that the DLPFC does not generate metacognitive contents directly, but rather regulates the executive and attentional processes that inform metacognitive evaluations.
Visual perception is assessed through both objective measures of perceptual performance and subjective reports of visual experience or confidence.

Objective perceptual performance can be quantified by discrimination sensitivity (d′), whereas subjective visibility refers to the perceived clarity or strength of a stimulus (e.g. seen/unseen judgments).

Importantly, subjective visibility and decision confidence are related but distinct constructs: visibility captures the quality of the perceptual experience itself, whereas confidence reflects the observer's subjective estimate of their decision's accuracy (Rausch & Zehetleitner, 2016; Mazor, Dijkstra & Fleming, 2022).

text.text: Metacognitive sensitivity, in turn, captures the extent to which subjective judgments distinguish correct from incorrect perceptual decisions, while metacognitive efficiency evaluates this sensitivity relative to underlying perceptual capacity (d') (Maniscalco & Lau, 2012; Fleming & Lau, 2014; Fleming, 2017).

text.text: Notably, these measures can dissociate: changes in subjective reporting do not necessarily entail corresponding shifts in objective performance, and metacognitive sensitivity can vary independently of first-order visual sensitivity (Maniscalco & Lau, 2016; Rausch & Zehetleitner, 2016).

text.text: Distinguishing subjective visibility from metacognitive sensitivity and efficiency is therefore important for determining whether an experimental manipulation alters the strength of subjective visual experience, the fidelity of metacognitive monitoring, or both.
Manipulating spatial attention provides a direct way to test these different aspects of vision.

While attending a stimulus location typically enhances objective perceptual performance (Posner, 1980; Posner, 2016; Chica et al., 2011), attention can also modulate subjective reports independently of changes in sensitivity.

text.text: Consequently, attention may change subjective visual experience, the efficiency with which subjective experience tracks objective performance, or both.
Here, we focus on endogenous or top-down spatial attention, in which centrally presented cues voluntarily direct attention toward an expected stimulus location.

While recent evidence indicates that endogenous attention can influence both perceptual performance and subjective judgments (Jurkiewicz et al., 2026; Krug & Huckauf, 2025; Fernández, Okun & Carrasco, 2021; Recht, Gardelle & Mamassian, 2021), the extent to which it distinctly modulates subjective visibility and metacognitive efficiency remains unresolved.

text.text: A persistent methodological challenge is that attention typically improves objective performance, making it difficult to determine whether changes in subjective measures reflect true attentional modulation or simply a byproduct of improved perception (Pruitt, Knotts & Odegaard, 2024).

text.text: To overcome this, we utilized adaptive staircasing to equate d' across valid and invalid cue conditions, allowing attentional effects on subjective visibility and metacognitive efficiency to be examined without altering basic perceptual performance.
A primary candidate mechanism for this top-down modulation is the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC).

The DLPFC is central to executive control, supporting the maintenance of task goals and the top-down regulation of visual regions to select behaviorally relevant information (Miller & Cohen, 2001; Paneri & Gregoriou, 2017).

text.text: These dual functions position the DLPFC as a critical nexus between top-down attentional control and the modulation of metacognitive awareness.

For example, Rounis et al. (2010) reported that disrupting the DLPFC reduced metacognitive sensitivity without affecting discrimination performance, though this interpretation has sparked ongoing debate (Bor et al., 2017; Ruby, Maniscalco & Peters, 2018; Martin, Lane, & Hsu, 2023).

text.text: It remains unclear whether DLPFC involvement extends from metacognitive monitoring to subjective visual experience, and whether it actively contributes to the attentional modulation of these processes.

This present pilot study provides an initial test of whether top-down spatial attention modulates subjective visibility and metacognitive efficiency independently of objective performance, and whether these effects depend on DLPFC function.
We tested these predictions across two experiments.
Experiment 1 utilized an endogenous Posner cueing task paired with metacontrast masking and adaptive staircasing.
We hypothesized that valid cues would facilitate attentional orienting, reflected in shorter reaction times, while objective sensitivity (d') would remain matched.
By equating basic performance, we aimed to determine whether spatial attention selectively enhances the efficiency of metacognitive monitoring, elevates overall subjective visibility, or both.

In Experiment 2, we applied continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS) over the bilateral DLPFC (or an active S1 control site) to establish a causal link between DLPFC function and these attention-dependent effects.
If the DLPFC mediates this top-down modulation, we predicted that cTBS disruption would attenuate cueing-related changes.

Finally, building on evidence that recent decision history shapes perceptual and metacognitive processing (Benwell et al., 2023), we conducted trial-by-trial analyses to explore how attentional history shapes these dynamics.

Four participants were excluded according to the criteria described below, leaving a final sample size of 15.
All participants had normal or correctedto-normal vision, provided written informed consent, and received monetary compensation.

Stimuli were presented using PsychoPy3 (v2021.2.3) on a 60-Hz LCD monitor in a dark room.

text.text: Each trial began with a 1000 ms fixation period followed by a spatial cue (600 ms) that validly predicted the target location on 70% of trials.
A briefly presented target (33 ms; square or diamond) appeared 3° to the left or right of fixation and was followed after a 50ms interstimulus interval by a metacontrast mask (50 ms).
Participants were asked to report if they had consciously seen the figure.

Participants identified the target shape while maintaining central fixation and simultaneously reported whether they consciously perceived the stimulus using a combined four-key response that encoded both discrimination accuracy (square/diamond) and subjective visibility (seen/unseen).
Participants were instructed to guess the target identity whenever they reported not seeing it.
The experiment began with two 100-trial practice stages using adaptive staircase procedures (Kaernbach, 1991).

Separate staircases were maintained for both valid and invalid cue trials to equate objective task performance across attention conditions.
The main experiment consisted of five blocks of 100 trials in which staircase adjustments continued to maintain stable performance.
Participants were asked to identify the shape of the target stimulus and report if they had seen it.

Visual and metacognitive performance was quantified using signal detection theory.

text.text: Across two experiments, we investigated whether endogenous spatial attention modulates subjective visibility and metacognitive efficiency while objective perceptual performance is controlled, and whether these effects depend on DLPFC function.

Experiment 1 showed that invalid spatial cues increased reaction times and reduced metacognitive efficiency without detectable changes in objective perceptual sensitivity or subjective visibility ratings.
These findings indicate that endogenous attention influences response speed and metacognitive performance beyond its effects on perceptual discrimination.
Experiment 2 provided preliminary evidence that the effects of cue validity on reaction times and metacognitive efficiency differed following DLPFC versus S1 stimulation.

Given the established role of the DLPFC in executive control and top-down attentional regulation (Miller & Cohen, 2001; Paneri & Gregoriou, 2017), these findings raise the possibility that prefrontal control processes mediate the influence of spatial attention on metacognitive performance.

text.text: Despite matched perceptual sensitivity, valid cues were associated with faster responses and greater metacognitive efficiency.

Together, these findings suggest that endogenous attentional orienting influences conscious reports through mechanisms extending beyond early sensory encoding, supporting the view that metacognitive judgements incorporate higher-order information in addition to perceptual evidence (Peng & Tullis, 2021; Sherman et al., 2015).

text.text: More broadly, our findings indicate that endogenous attention does not alter the overall conscious visibility of stimuli, but rather modulates how accurately observers' visibility reports track their own perceptual accuracy.

This aligns with prior work showing that spatial attention can improve visual performance without altering confidence ratings (Wilimzig et al., 2008), further highlighting the distinction between metacognitive performance and visual awareness (Jachs et al., 2015).

text.text: Experiment 2 provides preliminary causal evidence that this attentional modulation depends on the DLPFC.

Despite preserved objective performance and subjective reporting across stimulation conditions, DLPFC-cTBS attenuated the behavioural facilitation and metacognitive advantage associated with valid attentional orienting, which remained intact following control S1-cTBS.

This suggests that the DLPFC is necessary for translating topdown attentional cues into behavioral and metacognitive advantages, and for managing the trial-by-trial adjustments through which cognitive control adapts to changing attentional demands (MacDonald et al., 2000; Pulopulos et al., 2022).

text.text: While the observed behavioral and metacognitive facilitation in our study appears causally dependent on the DLPFC, the precise underlying neurocognitive processes require further characterization.
The role of the DLPFC as an executive controller, rather than a mere sensory conduit, is further supported by our sequential analyses.

Under control S1-cTBS conditions, we observed robust trial-by-trial adaptations: an invalid cue on the preceding trial temporarily blunted the metacognitive cueing effect and modulated current-trial reaction times.

This reflects a dynamic adjustment where violated prior expectations trigger a recalibration of cognitive control to handle changing attentional demands (MacDonald et al., 2000; Pulopulos et al., 2022).

text.text: Following DLPFC-cTBS, however, these sequential adaptations were abolished.
The cueing effect on metacognitive efficiency persisted indiscriminately even after invalid trials, and reaction time history effects disappeared.
Although preliminary, these data suggest that the DLPFC actively drives the trial-by-trial adjustment of attentional control based on recent cueing history.
When the DLPFC is disrupted, the brain fails to update its preparatory executive processes in response to prior errors.
By combining these main and sequential effects, our findings provide a potential framework to contextualize the mixed results regarding the DLPFC and visual metacognition.

Whereas Rounis et al. (2010) reported reduced metacognitive efficiency following DLPFC-cTBS, subsequent studies failed to replicate such a generalized impairment (Bor et al., 2017 (Bor et al., , 2018;; Martin et al., 2023).

text.text: Our preliminary findings help bridge these accounts: we observed no main effects of stimulation site on overall metacognition, suggesting the DLPFC is not a dedicated computational module for metacognition per se.
Instead, it may specifically support the executive processes through which top-down attentional cues influence the efficiency of metacognitive evaluations.

This perspective fits with broader evidence implicating the DLPFC in cognitive control, top-down attention, and cognitive flexibility, rather than in generating conscious perceptual contents or acting as an isolated metacognitive module (Gbadeyan et al., 2016; Ryali et al., 2016; Uddin, Yeo & Spreng, 2019; Lowe et al., 2018; Bor & Seth, 2012).

text.text: Given the complexity of metacognition, future research must prioritize investigating its interactions with other cognitive systems to delineate the exact role of prefrontal nodes in perception, confidence, and consciousness.
Several limitations should be acknowledged.
First, Experiment 2 was designed as a pilot study and included only seven participants.
The small sample inherently limits statistical power, resulting in considerable uncertainty regarding the estimated effects and their magnitudes.
The findings from Experiment 2 should be interpreted as preliminary, particularly for the effects assessed using the ART ANOVA.
The limited samples also complicates the interpretation of certain discrepancies between the two experiments.
For instance, in Experiment 1, participants exhibited a more conservative response bias (higher c′) following invalid cues.
This effect did not reach significance in Experiment 2, leaving it unclear whether the effect reflects a reliable modulation of the decision criterion or sampling variability.
Because participants in Experiment 2 had previously completed Experiment 1, task familiarity may also have contributed to this discrepancy.
Ultimately, the small sample of Experiment 2 limits the reliability of both null and positive findings, highlighting the critical need for replication in larger, independent cohorts.
Second, we quantified metacognitive efficiency using the method described by Maniscalco and Lau (2012), primarily to facilitate comparison with Rounis et al. (2010).

text.text: However, newer measures of metacognitive performance have been proposed (e.g. Fleming, 2017), each carrying distinct assumptions and potential sources of bias (Rahnev, 2025).

text.text: Our estimates should thus be contextualized within the specific metric employed, and future studies should assess the robustness of these effects across alternative modeling approaches.
Finally, because reaction times varied despite constant discrimination performance, our reaction time findings warrant cautious interpretation.
In research on unconscious processing and priming, reaction time is often utilized as an objective measure of sensory processing (Meyen et al., 2022).
text.formatted: In research on unconscious processing and priming, reaction time is often utilized as an objective measure of sensory processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Meyen et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, observing response speed modulations without d' changes raises important questions regarding the precise boundary between conscious and unconscious performance metrics in metacognition research.
This questions the distinction between conscious and unconscious performance in metacognition research.
In summary, our findings indicate that endogenous spatial attention modulates both reaction time and metacognitive efficiency without altering objective perceptual sensitivity.
Furthermore, our pilot cTBS experiment data provide preliminary evidence that this modulation depends on intact DLPFC function.

Rather than directly generating conscious perceptual contents or performing metacognitive evaluation, the DLPFC may contribute to visual metacognitive awareness through executive control processes that regulate attentional demands and the evaluation of perceptual decisions.
